articles.title: Gelato for lunch? Bedlinen in the freezer? Heatwave tips from southern Europe
articles.content:
With scorching temperatures breaking records across Europe this summer, The Local has put together tried and tested tips for surviving heatwaves from southern Europe, where locals have had decades of practice coping with the heat.

Several heatwaves have hit Europe so far this summer, breaking records in the process.

More than two-thirds of Europeans endured temperatures topping 35C during the June 15th-30th heatwave, according to an AFP analysis, and western Europe experienced its hottest June-July period on record.

Scientists have shown that recurring heatwaves are a clear marker of global warming, primarily caused by burning coal, oil and gas -- and warn they are set to become more frequent, longer and more intense.

READ ALSO: One for the history books - What we know about the European heatwave

Temperatures topping 40C have long been the case in traditionally sunny destinations of southern Europe - Spain, Italy, southern France - but now it's increasingly common in other countries not known for heatwaves: Austria, for example, recently recorded its highest temperature ever, with 41C registered in Vienna.

Even the 'hot' countries are breaking temperature records, and early summer heatwaves in France, Spain and Italy have led to increases in the excess death tolls, as well as heat-related problems like droughts and wildfires.

The Local recently covered the idea of 'coolcations' - the new trend of travelling north (think Sweden, or Scotland, or somewhere else with mild summer temperatures) during the hotter months.

But with average summer temperatures creeping up across Europe, perhaps now The Local's readers in northern Europe could use some tips from those in the south of the continent.

Here's a collection of advice and tips from our coverage in hotter countries putting together a combination of government advice and age-old tips passed on over the years.

We're going to take it as read that you know to drink plenty of water and stay hydrated in hot weather . . .

READ ALSO: Will heatwaves push European holidaymakers to 'coolcations'?

Spain, which just had its hottest month on record in July, has long been home to many heatwave management tips.

Spray water on curtains and bedsheets - While you don’t really want to go to bed soaked, lightly spraying your bed and your curtains with a fine mist can help.

The idea behind this is similar to the one above in that through evaporation, it helps cool the room down faster. 

Put your bedlinen in the freezer for a while - You’re probably using your freezer a lot more in the summer, to store and make ice, ice-creams, lollies and to keep drinks cool, but have you considered cooling down your sheets to help you sleep better?

You should typically leave them in for around 10-15 minutes. The freezing process removes heat from the fabric and provides a cool refreshing surface to lie down on. Be aware though, the sheets will turn to normal temperature within 15 to 20 minutes, but it might help you drift off to sleep at the start of the night.

Read the full breakdown of our sleeping in a Spanish heatwave tips below

READ ALSO: Twelve Spanish tricks to sleep better during a heatwave

Switch off lights- Of course most people sleep with the lights out anyway, but if you can turn them off well before you go to bed in your room, it can in fact lower the temperature by a couple of degrees. Every little helps when you’re trying to sleep in extreme heat right?

Wear loose clothing - However you choose to sleep in a heatwave, make sure you’re not wearing tight clothing that clings to your body. You want loose fitting garments that allow airflow to pass between them and your skin, which can speed up sweat evaporation and help keep you cooler.

Put an ice bucket in front of a fan - If you don’t have air-conditioning you can try creating your own DIY version by putting a bowl of ice in front of a fan to blow cooler air onto you.

This method works better in southern or central Spain where the heat is dryer. In more humid places such as along the Mediterranean coast, it can make the room feel stickier and may in fact make the situation worse.

If the summer heat is making you lose your appetite, the delicious Spanish food and drink specialties linked below will help fill you up whilst keeping you cool.

READ ALSO: The best Spanish food and drink to keep you cool during the summer heat

The Italian health ministry every year publishes a list of guidelines to keep cool and stay safe during a heatwave. These include tips on what to eat, how to dress and how to keep your place cool in the hottest hours of the day.

READ ALSO: 'Choose pasta or fish': Italy's official advice for keeping cool in a heatwave

If you just can’t endure scorching-hot temperatures and are looking for a way to flee the intense heat, the diversity of Italy's landscape means that you’ll find no shortage of ‘coolcation’ spots to choose from.

READ ALSO: Five articles to help you survive Italy’s heatwave

Of the ministry's advice, here's the best of the rest.

Spend the afternoon indoors - The health ministry's website advises staying inside between 11am to 6pm, when the sun is at its most intense.

While it's tempting when you're travelling to try and make the most of every minute, be sensible with your schedule: plan to hit museums, shops, restaurants or other indoor attractions in the afternoon and save outdoor sights for the early morning or evening, especially if they involve a lot of walking or don't offer shade – Pompeii, we're looking at you.

There is a reason that a post-lunch siesta remains popular in much of the country, at least in the summer months.

Eat light - Of course you've come to Italy to eat. But try not to overdo it on hot days, and don't even think of tackling a full antipasto-primo-secondo at lunch.

Italy's health ministry offers several pieces of food-focused advice, including to "moderate our consumption of dishes high in fat and reduce condiments."

The ministry also reminds us to "consume five portions of fruit and seasonal vegetables per day," and to generally "favour fresh produce that is easily digestible and rich in water."

READ ALSO: The Italian summer habits all foreigners should adopt

Take care in the car - Check the traffic report before setting off to see whether you're likely to be stuck in gridlock under the full sun.

Avoid driving during the heat of the day unless your vehicle has air conditioning, and make sure you carry extra water for the journey.

Never leave anyone, human or animal, in a car parked in the sun. When you're returning to a hot parked car, air it out or put on the air conditioning before setting off, and check that child seats aren't too hot to sit in.

Gelato for lunch? - In slightly more left-field advice, one of the ministry's official recommendations is to substitute lunch with a gelato.

"Consuming an ice cream or a milkshake can be an alternative to a midday meal," the guide suggests – just remember to factor it into your daily nutritional intake.

It also urges people to "be imaginative when preparing dishes" and "respect the correct number and timing of meals, without skipping breakfast".

The French government also offers advice to citizens on how to survive heatwaves.

READ ALSO: Light meals and shutters - The French government advice for surviving a heatwave

Avoid alcohol - In what seems surprisingly un-French advice, they say to avoid alcohol.

On a scorching day sometimes only the thought of an ice-cold pint gets you through, but the French government recommends avoiding alcohol. It will dehydrate you, so maybe at least drink in moderation if you can't resist a cheeky chilled rosé on a summer evening.

There are some great bière sans alcool (alcohol free beer) options available in France.

Be aware of the physical symptoms  - France's ministry of health also encourages people to be aware of the physical side effects that high temperatures can bring on. These include cramping, fatigue, headaches, fevers, nausea, and incoherent speech.

If you believe that you or someone you know could be experiencing heat stroke - particularly if fainting, incoherent speech or high fever is involved, then you should call the emergency number 15.

Avoid iced drinks- French experts also say to avoid iced drinks.

We all know that drinking plenty of water is vital when it's hot - but although iced water sounds like the most refreshing choice, it might not be as cooling as you think.

Why is it a bad idea? Drinking iced water won't do you any harm, but might cool you down less than un-iced water. The reason for this is that the stomach has temperature sensors, which when confronted with very cold liquids will instruct the body to warm up - which is not what you want.

Paris-based cardiologist Alain Ducardonnet told French TV channel BFM: "The ideal is to drink water at room temperature or a little cooler."

The French Ministry of Health also recommends avoiding sodas and sugary drinks, as well as those with high caffeine content as these have a diuretic effect (they make you pee) and are therefore dehydrating.

READ ALSO: 'Avoid iced water and air-conditioning on max' - How the French stay cool in a heatwave

articles.title: Who are the international residents most likely to leave Norway?
articles.content:
A significant proportion of foreign nationals who relocate to Norway eventually choose to leave the country, with departure rates varying according to the initial reason for immigration, as data from Statistics Norway (SSB) has revealed.

Of the 1,216,000 non-Nordic citizens who immigrated to Norway between 1990 and 2025, approximately 69 percent (844,000 individuals) remained registered as residents in the country as of January 1st 2026.

This indicates that nearly one-third of all international arrivals during the past three decades have since relocated elsewhere.

According to the SSB analysis, the likelihood of long-term residence in Norway is strongly influenced by the initial reason for immigration.

Foreigners arriving on education permits are the most likely to leave Norway. Only 37 percent of the 115,000 students who arrived between 1990 and 2025 remain in the country.

This outcome is primarily due to the requirement for graduates to obtain a new legal basis, such as a work permit, to remain after completing their studies, which presents significant challenges for long-term residence.

Foreign workers also frequently depart after several years.

Of the 398,000 migrant workers who arrived during the same 35-year period, 61 percent were still living in Norway at the beginning of 2026.

Individuals immigrating for family reunification show a greater tendency to settle long-term, with 76 percent of the 404,000 arrivals in this category still residing in Norway.

This is usually because they have stronger ties to Norway, whether through having a Norwegian partner or family already in the country.

Individuals seeking international protection are the most likely to remain in Norway on a permanent basis.

Of the 290,000 refugees who have arrived since 1990, 85 percent remain registered as residents.

READ ALSO: 'I can't say I wasn't warned': Why foreign residents leave Norway

While SSB data shows that the initial reason for moving can influence how long you stay, general feedback reveals that those who choose to leave Norway are also driven by a variety of other factors.

These factors typically include difficulties with social integration, feeling lonely, specific challenges encountered by healthcare professionals, and limited career or employment opportunities.

articles.title: Kinesiske handelsskip vil bruke sjøveien i nord på fast basis
articles.content:
Det kinesiske rederiet Sea Legend vil denne uken begynne å bruke Nordøstpassasjen på fast basis for å frakte varer vestover fra Asia.

Selskapet har døpt ruten «Issilkeveien» – en referanse til den 6000 kilometer lange Silkeveien som i oldtiden ble brukt til å frakte varer mellom øst og vest.

Ifølge Financial Times (FT) starter selskapet regulær skipstrafikk gjennom Arktis denne uken med et lasteskip som skal gå fra Ningbo på Kinas østkyst til Felixstowe i Storbritannia.

De islagte havområdene i nord har gjort det umulig å sende handelsskip fra Asia til Europa via Nordøstpassasjen, men som følge av global oppvarming og smelting av polarisen framstår ruten som et stadig mer realistisk alternativ til de mer tradisjonelle rutene lenger sør.

Kina

Kina er verdens nest mest folkerike land, og blant de eldste kontinuerlige sivilisasjonene i verden. Landet ledes av kommunistpartiet og president Xi Jinping, som er den første lederen siden formann Mao som har sittet i tre 5-årsperioder.

articles.title: Today in Norway: A roundup of the latest news on Monday
articles.content:
Trains cancelled between Oslo and Lillestrøm, landslide in Bergen, Conservative leader wants private agencies to help unemployed get work, and other news from Norway on Monday.

A fault on the track between Oslo and Lillestrøm led to a succession of cancelled trains on Monday morning, including several Flytoget departures to Oslo's Gardermoen Airport, the state-owned train company Vy has said on its website.

"There are fewer tracks to use in the Romeriksporten rail tunnel, so we are cancelling the L1 trains between Asker and Lillestrøm, and then the R13 trains between Lillestrøm and Oslo Central," Kaja Rynning Moen, a press officer for Vy, told the VG newspaper.

Norwegian vocabulary: togtrøbbel – train trouble/train disruptions

Norway political festival kicks off with school and unemployment proposals

Arendalsuka, or Arendal Week, Norway's annual political jamboree, kicked off today, with the Conservative leader Ine Eriksen Søreide calling for a public-private partnership on getting unemployed people jobs, and Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre calling for action to improve Norway's schools.

"We must dare to think new things," Søreide said of the proposal to get private recruitment agencies to work with the Norwegian Labour and Welfare Administration (NAV) to get more people into work.

"When Nav has as many tasks as they do, and does a very good job with many of those tasks, it will take less time to find a good match between a person who needs a job and a company that needs labour, if it is done by a staffing agency," she said.

Støre, meanwhile, on his second day back at work after his holiday, said that international studies showed that Norwegian children were reading less well, doing worse in maths, and writing less well.

"We must and will turn the tide,” he said, before the Minister of Education presented plans on how she wants to improve the knowledge of the country's students.

Norwegian athlete Jakob Ingebrigtsen back competing

The Norwegian runner Jakob Ingebrigtsen is returning to competition after almost a year in recovery, as he takes part in the European 5,000-metre Championships on Monday.

Ingebrigtsen, who took home a gold from the Paris Olympics in 2024, has not run competitively since the final of the 5000-metre World Championships in September last year, taking time off for surgery to fix problems with his Achilles tendon.

"I'm probably the person who's most excited. We made a decision that as long as my Achilles and body are 100 percent, there is no reason not to compete. Hopefully this championship will be a small stepping stone in terms of form towards the road ahead," he said at a press conference on Sunday.

Detention hearing for Crown Princess Mette-Marit's son

Marius Borg Høiby, the son of Crown Princess Mette-Marit, is in court on Monday as police request that his detention at home with an ankle bracelet be extended by four weeks.

Høiby has been in custody for over six months, but has spent the last period of his detention with an ankle bracelet at home in Skaugum, from where he has been allowed to travel to work, school, treatment or visits to sick family members.

Extremely heavy rain in Western Norway led to a series of landslides in the Bergen area on Sunday. Although several people had to evacuate, no one was injured.

On Sunday morning, emergency services rushed out to a landslide in a residential area in the Fana district of Bergen .

"Both the police and the fire department are on the scene," the operations manager in the Western Police District, Tore-Andre Brakstad, told VG. "As of now, three homes have been evacuated. This concerns one house on the lower side where the landslide occurred, and two houses on the upper side," he said.

According to the police, the landslide occurred between two houses, with the dislodged earth now partially resting on a detached house. Over the course of Sunday, four houses were evacuated, with residents returning to three of them by Sunday evening.

articles.title: Foreigners in Norway face '60 percent' lower chance of promotion
articles.content:
Norway has increasingly positioned itself as a top destination for international workers, yet a major new report revealed that the "career ladder" is significantly harder to climb for those with an immigrant background.

The report, "Ethnic Inequality in Working Life," commissioned by the Norwegian Directorate for Integration and Diversity (IMDi), unveiled a harsh reality for the international community living in the Nordic country.

The study examined how an ethnic minority background affects employees' opportunities in the Norwegian labour market.

It found that, despite securing employment, many foreigners face persistent barriers to career advancement, fair pay, and a safe work environment.

"Racism and discrimination are widespread and persistent problems in Norway, and we know that the consequences can be poorer living conditions and health. We should not have it this way. We need everyone who can work, and work is the most important integration arena we have," said Kjersti Stenseng the Minister of Employment and Inclusion.

For many international residents, these findings present a discouraging outlook for their long-term lives in Norway.

Although the Norwegian labour market is often praised for its egalitarianism, the data showed a significant disparity in who moves up.

Immigrants are 60 percent less likely to be promoted than other employees. This disparity is most pronounced among individuals with backgrounds from outside Europe and North America.

Those born in Norway, with a minority background are 30 percent less likely to be promoted, the report said.

According to the report the work environment for international residents is often affected by their background.

A higher proportion of immigrants reported experiencing bullying or harassment at work in the past 12 months compared to the majority population.

These rates are significantly higher among certain groups, especially those from Africa and Asia, and particularly among refugees.​

READ MORE: Is mastering Norwegian now a must for getting a job in Norway?

​Many international workers in Norway find themselves stuck in roles for which they are overtrained.

The report found that immigrants are 5 to 7 percentage points more likely to be overqualified for their current position compared to the rest of the population.

Researchers suggested this mismatch often results from challenges in recognising foreign education and qualifications in Norway, as well as potential discrimination in how tasks are allocated within the workplace.

Interestingly, this gap disappears for the children of immigrants (second generation) who are born and raised in Norway.

For those who have immigrated themselves, however, finding work that matches their actual skills and experience is slow.

The research highlighted that it takes about 20 years in the Norwegian labour market for the overqualification gap to close.

This gradual improvement is linked to foreign-born residents acquiring stronger Norwegian language skills and relevant work experience in the local market.

As the report stated: "It is natural to assume that over-qualification is linked to the arrival phase and the first years in the Norwegian labour market, as well as to unobserved differences in language skills that we can assume become smaller with longer residence. The patterns are approximately identical for immigrants regardless of region of origin".

Regarding psychosocial work environment factors, immigrants reported slightly less social support from colleagues but receive equal or better follow-up from managers.

While these findings focus on those already in jobs, previous research has also documented that people are treated differently during the initial hiring processes based on their ethnic background.

The report identifies a wage difference of 12 percent between employees with an immigrant background and the rest of the population.

However, researchers emphasise that this disparity is mainly because employees with an immigrant background are more likely to end up working in companies and businesses with lower pay scales.

Meaning the gap could be due to "selection", as it shrinks to about 2 percent when comparing employees in the same position at the same workplace.

Notably, wage gaps are smaller in the public sector compared to the private sector.

This is mainly because the public sector follows more standardised wages, leaving less room for subjective employer discrimination or individual negotiation.

The gaps are also smallest in highly regulated professions with clear authorisation requirements.

In addition to career advancement, the report found significant disparities in job stability and safety.

Immigrants in Norway face higher job insecurity, reporting a greater perceived risk of unemployment in the near future compared to the majority population.

Also, while overall differences in the physical work environment are small, immigrants are more likely to perform heavy physical labour.

Researchers noted that the combined impact of these 'hard' outcomes (including higher rates of bullying, long-term sick leave, and limited institutional infrastructure to protect workers, such as Health, Safety, and Environment - HSE schemes) suggests a much harsher reality for many international workers.

These factors indicate that immigrants often face a more stressful work environment with a greater risk of illness and injury.

READ MORE: Norway offers renowned work-life balance, so why are so many suffering burnouts?

Can employers do more to create equal opportunities?

The research identified measures that can reduce the risk of workplace discrimination.

Experts recommend moving away from standard employee training, which was found ineffective at changing attitudes or behaviour.

Instead, structural changes should be considered, such as inclusive career systems and access to mentors.

articles.title: Do Norway's 'språkkafé' language cafés actually work?
articles.content:
The concept of 'språkkafé', or language cafés, has gained popularity in Norway as a way to connect with local people and practise your Norwegian. How do these social spaces for foreigners actually help, what can you get out of them, and are they worth your time?

The process of learning Norwegian can be a lonely one. Spending hours on Duolingo or with textbooks doesn’t always help you feel confident in real conversations. Many foreigners share the same frustration: “I understand way more than I can actually speak.”

People might comprehend the news and decipher signs, but when it’s time to talk, they freeze.

To help with this gap and break out of the 'English bubble', foreigners are often encouraged to try språkkafé (languaje café) events. But do they really help, or are they just a social Band-Aid?

New to the concept? Read What is a 'Språkkafé' and why is it so popular in Norway?

People in the international community have mixed opinions. For some, språkkafés are life-changing. For others, it can feel like “the blind leading the blind” if there aren’t enough native speakers to interact with.

Vendula Hurnik Åtland, a Project Leader in Gamle Oslo who coordinates the Språkkafé at Deichman Tøyen (an initiative organised by Tøyen Frivilligsentral), noted: “I wouldn’t say you can learn the language only by attending, but it’s a great place to put your knowledge to the test.”

For many learners, the results are undeniable. The café helps people overcome their fear of speaking. In fact, some have even reached intermediate levels and credited the meetups for much of their progress.

Vignesh Jeyaraman, from India, who has lived in Norway for four years, said: “I am proud to say that all the Norwegian I speak today, which is at a B1 level, I learned there. I never attended a formal course, so the language café helped me a lot. My Norwegian isn’t perfect, but I can hold a conversation comfortably.”

For those who cannot afford expensive private courses, the café is a vital resource. “People who attend are definitely motivated,” said Åtland. “For some, it’s their only way to try and learn.”

The main criticism comes up when there aren’t enough native speakers. One participant explained, “It’s not always a great experience; there are hardly any natives. Speaking only to other learners can feel like the blind leading the blind.”

Jean-François Chou, a regular attendee from France who has lived in Norway for 5 years, said these spaces are for practice, not for primary learning.

He suggests a more strategic approach: “I always recommend cafés with a higher ratio of Norwegians to foreigners. If the volunteer speaks for 60 minutes and you sit with six other foreigners, you might only get 10 minutes of actual practice.”

He is especially critical of larger groups. “You sit with 6-8 other foreigners. The Norwegian volunteer will lead the discussion, but in reality, you practice more with other learners than with a native.” He suggested looking for smaller venues, like Paulus Kirke in Oslo, which often have more locals.

For many people, the real value of a språkkafé goes beyond verbs and pronunciation. It’s also a kind of therapy. These spaces help people deal with the emotional challenges of starting a new life.

Murat Sarayli, from Turkey, who has lived in Norway for 10 years, described the impact firsthand.  “I see it as a platform serving more than just language: språkkafés are therapy zones,” Murat said. “It is one of the rare places where immigrants can look into the eyes of locals who are devoting their time with empathy.”

Åtland agreed and said these spaces are essential for people who feel isolated: “There are a lot of people who are alone, and not only older people. This is a way of not only learning Norwegian and getting integrated, but also building a network.”

This sentiment is shared by Fernanda, who found solace in a Women’s Language Café. “It helped me so much,” she said. “Even when I didn’t understand everything, I felt integrated.”

This sense of community lets people share "tips and tricks" for living in Norway. “When you put people together with a common interest in getting a better life here, they share information about work and how to make friends. That counts just as much as the language,” said  Åtland. They also share advice on “how to just make the best out of living in Norway, or just making friends—this is important.”

Many people have this experience. For most, their closest friends in Norway are people they met at a språkkafé. Usually, these friendships are with other foreigners who also want to improve their language skills, but some people also make lasting connections with Norwegian volunteers. At the end of the day, a support network is vital.

For many internationals, going to a café is often the only regular way to meet Norwegians. Åtland pointed out that many expats work or study in English and just don’t meet locals.

“We have all been through that. The café is a good opportunity to actually meet Norwegians,” she said. As the level of Norwegian improves, the conversations evolve: “At the higher levels, they ask spicy questions about Norwegian culture, what locals think, and even politics.”

“My experience has been amazing,” said Vignesh. “I met amazing mentors and learned things about the culture. It’s the place where you get to meet natives; otherwise, it’s just too hard to meet people in this country.”

Åtland said: "We talk about Norwegian history, culture, or just practical things, like the fact that you have the right to a translator at the doctor. It’s those tiny details that make people's lives better."

“I learned about DNT hikes, NRK shows, and the apps Norwegians actually use,” Vignesh said.

However, for Jean-François, the value of the café remains tied to how many Norwegians are present. "In some språkkafés, where you discuss Norwegian culture with other non-natives, I feel it’s not the best," he noted.

Interestingly, for participants, the journey doesn't have to end with just attending. Becoming a volunteer can be a smart step.

“We have now two volunteers that help out with making the room ready before Språkkafé and then they attend the activity." said Åtland. “They get to talk for an extra hour with the Norwegian volunteers while working together. It’s a great way to get working experience and references for your CV and applications.”

If you’re thinking about going to a språkkafé, experienced attendees say success comes from making smart choices and sticking with it.

Vignesh said the most important thing is to trust the process. It can be frustrating at first, especially if you don’t even know the three extra Norwegian vowels, but if you keep going, it pays off.

"I am horrible with languages, but after three years, I can express my hobbies and feelings. If I can do it, anyone can," he said.

It’s also important to know when to start. Jean-François suggested that språkkafé becomes more rewarding once you reach at least the A2 level. “B1 is where the benefits are best because you can start to carry an actual discussion,” he noted.

He also advised newcomers to choose sessions with more Norwegians than foreigners.

Other participant offered a more blunt piece of advice: "Do not have great expectations."

If you decide to attend, consistency is key. As Jean-François concluded: "Going is always better than not going. I’ve been attending for over six months, every week, and the consistent effort has been very valuable."​

articles.title: Tyfon har truffet Kina – over én million evakuert
articles.content:
Over én million mennesker er evakuert etter at tyfonen Dolphin traff den østlige delen av Kina søndag, opplyser landets myndigheter.

Tyfonen bringer med seg kraftig regn, og ifølge myndighetene øker det risikoen for oversvømmelser og jordskred – særlig i landets fjellrike områder og langs elvene.

Kinesiske meteorologer har varslet at det kan komme 200–400 millimeter nedbør enkelte steder de neste dagene.

To flyplasser i Shanghai har søndag innstilt 1300 flyvninger som følge av stormen.

Varselet om kraftig regn gjelder fram til mandag i store deler av Øst-Kina.

Kina

Kina er verdens nest mest folkerike land, og blant de eldste kontinuerlige sivilisasjonene i verden. Landet ledes av kommunistpartiet og president Xi Jinping, som er den første lederen siden formann Mao som har sittet i tre 5-årsperioder.

articles.title: Zelenskyj: Odesas havn skadet i russiske angrep
articles.content:
Havnebyen Odesa i Ukraina ble truffet av russiske angrep natt til søndag. Åtte personer ble såret.

– Russerne fører krig mot verdens matsikkerhet, sier Ukrainas president Volodymyr Zelenskyj om nattens angrep.

Havnen i Odesa er hovedpulsåren for Ukrainas landbrukseksport.

De siste sesongene har Ukraina stått for omtrent 6 prosent av verdens hveteeksport og 11 prosent av den globale kornproduksjonen.

Langvarige forstyrrelser av landets eksport via Svartehavet utgjør en stor risiko for importavhengige land i Afrika og Asia.

Krigen i Ukraina

Russland invaderte Krim og deler av fylkene Luhansk og Donetsk i Øst-Ukraina i 2014. 24. februar 2022 gikk Russland til fullskala invasjon. Krigen medfører store militære tap og rammer sivile hardt.

articles.title: Siktet for ransforsøk i Ullensaker – fengslet i fire uker
articles.content:
En mann i begynnelsen av 20-årene ble lørdag varetektsfengslet i fire uker, siktet for flere lovbrudd, blant annet et ransforsøk.

– Det er en siktelse som gjelder forsøk på ran, et forhold som er begått i Ullensaker på fredag. I tillegg så er det trusler mot politiet samme dag, sier politiadvokat Julie Dahlsveen til NRK.

Mannen skal ha forsøkt å rane til seg en bil med kniv. Han er også siktet for å ha båret kniv og murstein tidligere samme dag.

Han har også flere eldre saker registrert på seg hos Innlandet politidistrikt, sier Dahlsveen.

I kjennelsen fra Hedmarken og Østerdal tingrett kommer det frem at retten deler påtalemyndighetens vurdering om at det er en fare for gjentakelse, og viser til mannens egne uttalelser og hvordan en fornærmet opplevde siktede.

– Retten viser til at siktedes ønske om å være på frifot må vike av hensyn til samfunnsvernet, står det i kjennelsen.
